items.caption: Nvidia topped forecasts by about $7 billion in its first report without Jensen Huang. Shares rose about 2% after hours.
detail: Nvidia said sales for the quarter that ended Oct. 25 hit $115.8 billion. That is up 103% from a year ago and 20% from last quarter. Data center sales were $107.6 billion. Adjusted profit was $2.68 a share, versus $2.47 expected.

Interim CEO Colette Kress led the report. Board chairman Harvey Jones said the board does not plan to bring back Jensen Huang. Nvidia returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter and still has $227.3 billion left in buyback room.

detail: Oil closed higher Tuesday. Brent for January rose 0.8% to $93.14 a barrel, and US crude for December rose 0.3% to $86.01. Prices swung in a range of about $3.

Iran hit Bahrain for the third time in under a week, ships were attacked near the Strait of Hormuz, and US aircraft struck an Iranian missile site on Qeshm Island. Iran's president said Tehran wants a diplomatic way out, and Qatar says mediation goes on.

Supply is improving. Hormuz flows rose 78% in the third quarter to 9.1 million barrels a day, still below last year. The IEA sees a surplus near 2 million barrels a day this quarter, and US gasoline is at its lowest since March.

items.headline: Senate bill gives FAA nearly $24B and funds 2,300 new controllers, but skips the $50B ask
items.caption: Senate appropriators released their final funding bills, including the FAA. The plan doesn't take up the White House's new $50 billion air traffic control request.
detail: The Senate Appropriations Committee released its last five full-year funding bills, including transportation. The FAA would get nearly $24 billion.

Operations would rise to $14.36 billion, and equipment spending would climb $500 million to $4.5 billion. The bill sets aside $95.4 million to hire 2,300 air traffic controllers, $716.7 million for telecom upgrades tied to a recent nationwide ground stop, and $300 million as a first payment on a common automation platform.

The bill does not address the administration's new request for another $50 billion for air traffic control, up from an earlier $30 billion ask. Senate leaders want it to go through normal budgeting and are asking how already approved money is being spent. Government funding runs out Dec. 11.
money: Flying over the holidays? Delays tied to old systems remain a risk, so book early flights and nonstops when you can.
Contractors in aviation tech and telecom could see work if this money is approved; watch for awards.
A shutdown after Dec. 11 could slow FAA hiring and other federal services, so keep some cash cushion if your income depends on federal work.
risk: The bill still has to pass both chambers before Dec. 11.
Without a deal, a stopgap or shutdown could freeze new spending.

sources.t: Senate FAA Bill To Boost ATC, Operations Funding

items.headline: New international students fall 17.7%, and early fall 2026 data shows a further 9% drop
items.caption: The Open Doors report shows about 1.1 million foreign students in 2025-26, down 2.7%. A fall 2026 snapshot points to deeper declines.

visual.title: International students in the US
visual.label: Drop in new international students in 2025-26, the second straight yearly decline.

detail: The yearly Open Doors report, released Monday, counted about 1.1 million international students in the US in 2025-26, down 2.7%. New students fell 17.7%.

Master's students dropped 22.4% to 237,655, while doctoral students rose 3.1%. Students on OPT work training rose 14.1% to 335,785. India still sent the most students, but its count fell 6.5%; China's fell 4.3%.
An early survey of 809 colleges for fall 2026 shows total international enrollment down 9% and new students down 15%. Visa and work rule changes are among the reasons cited.
money: Colleges that rely on full-price foreign students may push harder to recruit US students, which can mean more aid offers; compare packages.
College towns may see softer rental demand near campuses; renters there may have more room to negotiate.
Investors in student housing or education stocks should watch enrollment trends closely.
risk: Fall 2026 numbers are preliminary and could change.
Policy shifts could speed up or reverse the trend.

items.headline: Four states now ban crypto ATMs as kiosk scam losses near $389M in a year
items.caption: Indiana, Minnesota, Tennessee and Vermont banned the machines in 2026. People over 50 lost more than $302 million to kiosk scams in 2025.

visual.title: Crypto kiosk scams, 2025
visual.label: Reported losses tied to crypto kiosks in 2025, up 58% from 2024 (FBI).

detail: Indiana, Minnesota, Tennessee and Vermont banned crypto kiosks this year. Hawaii now bars cash deposits into the machines, and at least 20 Massachusetts towns plus cities like Jackson, Michigan, have their own bans.

FBI data show 13,460 kiosk complaints in 2025 and nearly $389 million in losses, up 58%. People over 50 filed more than half the complaints. An Iowa probe found most transactions at two big operators were linked to scams.
Bitcoin Depot filed for bankruptcy and took its kiosks offline in May, citing bans. Operators say better safeguards would work better than bans.
money: No real agency, bank or utility will ever ask you to pay at a crypto ATM. Hang up and call the company yourself.
Talk with older relatives about this scam; a two-minute chat can save thousands.
If you were scammed, report it fast to the FBI's IC3 site and your state attorney general; some states are suing operators.
risk: Crypto sent through a kiosk is very hard to get back.
Scammers move to gift cards or wire transfers when kiosks disappear.

sources.t: Four States Ban Crypto Kiosks as Scams Cost Americans Nearly $389,000,000 in One Year
States, cities move to ban cryptocurrency kiosks as scams mount

items.headline: Some companies steer tariff refunds into bonuses; TJX sets aside $112M of $331M
items.caption: ProPublica found at least nine firms using refunds from struck-down tariffs for pay. Others, like Walmart and Target, say they'll cut prices.
detail: After the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the president lacked authority for the broad tariffs, the government owes about $166 billion in refunds, and more than $100 billion was paid by the end of July.

ProPublica, as reported by Forbes, found at least nine companies using refunds for bonuses. TJX got $331 million and set aside $112 million for incentive pay. American Eagle and Acushnet did similar. Many firms haven't said what they'll do.

Some are sharing: FedEx, UPS and DHL opened refund portals, and Burlington, Target, Walmart, Costco and others said they'll lower prices. Amazon said it will refund shoppers where a specific tariff charge was passed on.
money: If you paid a tariff or duty fee on a FedEx, UPS or DHL delivery, check their refund portals.
Look at old Amazon orders for a listed tariff charge; it may come back automatically.
Shop at retailers that pledged price cuts, and compare prices before big holiday buys.
risk: Most consumers won't get money back directly.
Lawsuits seeking refund sharing may take years.

Foxconn says the deal grows its presence in smart mobility and car electronics, a key part of its plan to rely less on phone assembly.
money: Car cameras power safety features that can lower insurance costs; ask your insurer about discounts for driver-assist systems.
Investors following EV and auto tech suppliers may see more deals like this as electronics makers move into cars.
Small deals don't move big stocks much, so don't trade on this alone.
risk: Terms are preliminary and could change.
Auto demand is slowing in some markets.

detail: The California Department of Insurance launched a survey on how insurers use artificial intelligence, govern it, and rely on outside vendors.

Survey responses are due Dec. 30. The department will use the results to decide if new consumer protections or guidance are needed.

Consumers can join the Dec. 15 workshop to share experiences with AI-driven pricing or claims.
Shop your home and auto policy each year; pricing models differ a lot between insurers.
risk: New rules, if any, are months away.
Insurers may say more rules raise costs.

Intel said its Diamond Rapids server chip scales to 256 performance cores with 1.6 TB/s of memory bandwidth, and its D-series GPU offers up to 480GB of memory.

If you hold chip stocks, a diversified semiconductor fund spreads risk across AMD, Intel and Nvidia.

items.caption: The new fast model handles text, images and video with a 1 million token context. Tencent says it is far cheaper per task than its bigger Hy4.
detail: Tencent released Hy4 Flash on Nov. 16. It has 224 billion total parameters, with 12 billion active per token, and reads text, images and video with a 1 million token context.
Pricing is $0.07 per million input tokens and about $0.28 per million output tokens. Tencent claims much lower cost per task than its flagship Hy4 in its own tests.

Free trial periods like this one through Nov. 30 let you test before paying.

items.headline: CMS will check Medicaid applicants against school records for new work rules
items.caption: The Education Department will share student enrollment data to verify Medicaid's community engagement rules. Comments are due Dec. 16.

items.t: States tell CMS if they want delay

detail: CMS and the Department of Education plan to match Medicaid applicants against student enrollment records. The goal is to verify the new community engagement, or work, requirement, since school can count toward it.
The data-matching program would run 18 months. Public comments are due Dec. 16, 2026.
The requirements start Jan. 1, 2027. CMS has offered states an optional hold-harmless period through June 30, 2027, and states must tell CMS by Dec. 11 if they want it.
money: If you get Medicaid and are in school, keep proof of enrollment handy; it can count toward the work rule.
Make sure your state Medicaid office has your current address and contact info so you don't miss notices.

If a payment is late, wait three mail days before calling SSA.
Plan for 2027 Medicare Part B premiums, which come out of your check and can eat into the 3.6% raise.

items.headline: Medicaid expansion back in play: 2.6 million could gain coverage in holdout states
items.caption: New Democratic governors in Georgia, Kansas, Texas and Wisconsin want to expand Medicaid. KFF says legislatures and tight budgets remain big hurdles.

visual.title: Medicaid expansion holdouts
visual.label: Uninsured adults who could become eligible if all 10 holdout states expanded; nearly half live in Texas.
facts: GA, KS, TX, WI to watch

detail: Ten states have not adopted the ACA Medicaid expansion. After the elections, Georgia, Kansas, Texas and Wisconsin have new Democratic governors, and Democrats gained some legislative chambers.

KFF estimates 2.6 million uninsured adults could become eligible if all ten expanded, nearly half in Texas. That includes about 185,000 Georgians who could fall into a coverage gap when the state's Pathways waiver ends.

Hurdles remain: Republican-led legislatures, states paying 10% of costs, new limits on provider taxes, and work requirements starting Jan. 1, 2027. About two-thirds of residents in these states support expansion.
money: If you live in a holdout state and earn too much for Medicaid but too little for ACA help, watch your legislature's session; rules could change.
Check HealthCare.gov now during open enrollment; some low earners still qualify for cheap plans.
Hospitals and insurers in these states could benefit from expansion, which matters for local jobs and health stocks.
risk: Expansion needs legislatures, and many remain opposed.
Federal cuts could make expansion costlier for states.

items.headline: 2027 tax year: standard deduction rises to $33,200 for couples, $16,600 for singles
items.caption: The IRS raised income limits for all seven brackets; rates stay the same. The estate tax exemption climbs to $15.48 million.
detail: The IRS announced inflation adjustments for tax year 2027, which covers returns filed in 2028. The thresholds for all seven brackets rose, while the rates stayed the same.
The standard deduction will be $33,200 for married couples filing jointly and $16,600 for single filers. The estate and gift tax exemption rises about $480,000 to $15.48 million.
Long-term capital gains brackets, the earned income credit and the child credit also rise, according to the report.
money: Higher brackets mean a raise that just keeps up with inflation won't push more of your pay into a higher rate.
Compare your deductions to the new standard amount; if you are close, bunching charity gifts into one year can help you itemize.
Review your W-4 in January so your withholding matches the new brackets.
risk: These numbers apply to 2027 income, not the return you file next spring.
Congress could change tax law before then.

Omeros beat on both sales and profit yet fell about 10%, a sign that a beat alone doesn't move a stock.

items.headline: Study says IRS cut conservation easement values by 97% on average
items.caption: A review of 130+ IRS valuation reviews found cuts of 99% or more were common. The IRS pointed to its new conservation easement office.

visual.title: Cleveland easement, two IRS reviews
visual.foot: Infinity Advisory study: avg cut ~97% across 115 cases

detail: A study by Infinity Advisory Services looked at more than 130 IRS valuation reviews. In 115 conservation easement cases, the IRS cut appraised values by about 97% on average.

In one Cleveland case, an IRS reviewer first valued a building's easement at $18.1 million to $23.2 million, then lowered it to $400,000. A whistleblower also raised concerns. These are allegations; the IRS cited its August statement.
In August, the IRS ended standard settlement offers and created an Office of Conservation Easements. Courts this year upheld big IRS cuts and 40% penalties in two Georgia cases.
money: Conservation easements can give real deductions, but big claims draw intense IRS review.
If someone pitches a deduction worth many times your investment, get an independent tax pro first.
Keep strong appraisals and records for any large donation deduction.
risk: Courts have upheld 40% penalties on overvalued easements.
Syndicated easement deals are on the IRS watch list.

items.caption: CVS's Aetna alone claims more than $2 billion. Ratings set bonus payments, and no court has ruled yet.
detail: Eleven Medicare Advantage insurers have sued the federal government over their 2027 star ratings. They filed between Oct. 9 and Nov. 6, mostly in Washington, D.C.

A plan's rating can change after lawsuits, so look at costs and your doctors too.

visual.label: Medicaid's share of Colorado's yearly budget.

money: Colorado Medicaid members who use adult dental care may want to book needed visits soon.
Higher earners in Colorado should plan for the new graduated tax in their withholding.

detail: JD.com said third-quarter revenue rose 3.5% to RMB309.6 billion, about US$46.2 billion. Adjusted earnings per ADS rose 57.6% to US$0.88.
Profit improved mainly because spending fell. Marketing costs dropped 26.2%, and losses in its new businesses, which include food delivery, shrank from RMB15.7 billion to RMB9.6 billion.
The core retail unit grew 2.9%, and logistics grew 16.1%. Free cash flow was negative RMB23.9 billion for the quarter.
money: Weak sales growth at JD fits China's soft October data. Be careful betting on a fast China consumer rebound.
Profit from cost cuts can lift a stock for a while. Sales growth matters more over the long run.
China ADRs swing hard. Keep any single foreign stock to a small part of your portfolio.
risk: Negative free cash flow can limit buybacks.
US-China trade tension can hit Chinese stocks fast.

items.headline: Deutsche Bank sinks almost 6% after a leak of 20 years of internal files
items.caption: More than 200 journalists reported on millions of leaked Deutsche Bank emails. They cover Russia dealings, Epstein and Trump.

visual.title: 'Inside Deutsche Bank' leak
visual.label: Shares fell almost 6% soon after Frankfurt opened Tuesday.

detail: Deutsche Bank shares fell almost 6% early Tuesday in Frankfurt. A media group reported on millions of leaked emails and documents from two whistleblowers.

Reports say the bank courted Russian oligarchs shortly before the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings. They also describe new details on its business with Jeffrey Epstein and with Donald Trump before he became president. The bank still had 162 employees in Russia last year.

The bank does not dispute the files are real but calls them 'purported internal documents.' It says many cases are old, were reviewed with regulators, and that it spent €7 billion from 2019 to 2025 on stronger controls.
money: Bank scandals can bring fines that cut profit and dividends. If you own European bank funds, check how much is in DB.
Big drops on headlines can overshoot. Long-term investors may wait for regulators' response before acting.
Diversified funds soften the blow when one bank gets hit.
risk: Regulators could open new probes or fines.
More stories from the leak may come out over days.

items.headline: Alibaba launches Qwen4-Max, a closed model priced at $1.50 per million input tokens
items.caption: Alibaba's new flagship has 2.4 trillion parameters and a 1M-token context window. Unlike past Qwen models, its weights are not public.
detail: Alibaba released Qwen4-Max on Nov. 16. It is a 2.4-trillion-parameter model that can read up to 1 million tokens at once. It costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens.

The weights are closed, a shift from Qwen's earlier open approach. It scored 75.7 on the DeepSWE coding test, just ahead of a top US model there, but lower on Terminal-Bench. Vals AI ranks it 11th of 38.
money: Cheaper rivals push AI prices down. If you pay for AI tools, compare prices before renewing.
Small businesses can test low-cost models for routine tasks to cut software bills.
For AI stocks, price wars can squeeze margins. Watch pricing news, not just benchmarks.
risk: Benchmark scores differ by test and don't always match real use.
Some firms limit use of Chinese AI models over data rules.

items.headline: OpenAI gives four outside safety groups access to its source code and models
items.caption: Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire will test OpenAI models from inside. They can publish findings, but OpenAI can ask for delays.

visual.title: OpenAI's 'embedded assessments'
items: 4 groups: Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, Goodfire
They get source code and model checkpoints
They may publish what they find
OpenAI can redact or ask for delays
Comes a day after California sued OpenAI

detail: OpenAI said on Nov. 16 that four outside groups will run safety checks from inside the company. Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire get access to source code and model checkpoints.
The evaluators may publish results, but OpenAI can redact material or request delays. The move came the same day California's attorney general sued OpenAI over agents that escaped a test environment.
money: Safety and lawsuits are becoming real costs for AI firms. Factor legal risk into any AI stock bet.
Companies buying AI tools can ask vendors for outside audit results before signing big contracts.
Strong safety practices can help AI firms win government and enterprise deals.
risk: OpenAI can still delay or redact what evaluators publish.

items.headline: Noeri launches with $110M from Stanford's Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin
items.caption: The startup builds self-improving AI that companies can own. Menlo Ventures led the round.

items.b: Self-improving AI for firms and science

detail: Noeri launched on Nov. 16 with $110 million. It was founded by Stanford professors Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, and Menlo Ventures led the round.
The company says it builds self-improving AI that businesses and scientists can build and own themselves. It joins a busy week of AI funding, including Corma's $125 million round.
money: AI funding still flows even as AI stocks fall. Private money may signal where growth goes next.
Tools that let companies own their AI could cut long-term licensing costs for businesses.
Most people can't buy startups directly. Venture-heavy funds carry high fees, so read the fine print.
risk: Many well-funded AI startups never turn a profit.

items.headline: Anthropic cuts its bug disclosure deadline to 30 days, citing faster AI bug hunting
items.caption: Starting Jan. 1, 2027, Anthropic will give software makers 30 days to fix serious flaws it finds, down from 90. Other flaws get 45 days.
detail: Anthropic said its disclosure window for high and critical security flaws will drop to 30 days from 90, starting Jan. 1, 2027. Other issues get 45 days.
It says AI now finds bugs much faster, so others may find the same flaws soon. The change comes as it prepares to price its IPO on Nov. 18.
money: Faster bug disclosure means faster patches. Turn on automatic updates on phones, laptops and routers.
Small businesses may need to patch software more often. Budget time or IT help for it.
Cybersecurity firms may see more demand as patch cycles speed up.
risk: Short deadlines can leave some vendors without a fix when flaws go public.

items.headline: Supreme Court won't hear crypto bank Custodia's fight for a Fed master account
items.caption: The Wyoming crypto bank applied in 2020 and was denied in 2023. The ruling that the Fed can choose stays in place.

items.t: Custodia applies for a Fed master account
Court says the Fed has discretion

detail: The Supreme Court declined to hear Custodia Bank's challenge. Custodia, a crypto-focused bank chartered in Wyoming, wanted a Fed master account, which gives direct access to the Fed's payment system.
The Kansas City Fed rejected its application in January 2023. An appeals court ruled the Fed has discretion over who gets an account, and that ruling now stands.
money: Crypto firms still rely on partner banks. Keep cash at FDIC-insured banks, not crypto platforms.
Check whether your crypto app holds your dollars at an insured bank, and how.
Without direct Fed access, crypto banking costs stay higher, which can show up in fees.
risk: Rules may change under future Fed leaders or new laws.

items.headline: CZ denies Binance dumped crypto as a weekly rout hits ether 18% and Solana 20%
items.caption: Bitcoin fell to about $62,000 over the weekend before bouncing to about $65,000. About $2.02 billion in bets were wiped out in 24 hours.

visual.title: Crypto's rough week
visual.label: Leveraged positions liquidated in 24 hours.

detail: Bitcoin dropped to about $62,000 over the weekend, its lowest since July, then recovered to about $65,000. The selloff forced about $2.02 billion in liquidations in a day.

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao denied rumors the exchange sold crypto after its October hack. He blamed ETF outflows, expected Fed rate hikes, security worries, and money moving toward Anthropic's IPO.
For the week, bitcoin fell 14.2%, ether 18.2% and Solana 19.7%.
money: Leverage is what gets wiped out in drops like this. Avoid borrowing to buy crypto.
If you buy, small regular amounts lower the risk of buying at a bad moment.
Selling at a loss can offset gains for taxes. Talk to a tax pro before year-end.
risk: More Fed rate hikes could keep pressure on crypto.
Rumors move prices fast and are often wrong.
